evidence.label: Chapter opening: error probabilities concern the entire collection-and-stopping procedure
def:p15-se-model: observed information F_m = sigma(X_1..X_m) with trivial initial information; p_im, L_m and the singular-ratio conventions (Wald p.127)

def:p15-se-procedure: terminal regions R_m^0, R_m^1 and continuation region R_m on length-m histories; first terminal stage T with {T<=m} in F_m; decision measurable at stopping; actual errors alpha'=P_0(Q_1), beta'=P_1(Q_0) kept distinct from targets; nontermination a separate outcome; seed in initial information; fixed sample as the special case (Wald Sec. 2.1 p.123, Sec. 2.3 pp.124-125, Sec. 3.1 p.125)
thm:p15-se-posterior: posterior-odds motivation of the two ratio boundaries, kept distinct from frequentist calibration (Wald Sec. 3.1, (3.1)-(3.7), pp.125-126)
annex:p15.se.posterior proof
def:p15-se-sprt: accept H1 at L_m>=A, H0 at L_m<=B, continue in between; log form T=inf{m: Z_m not in (b,a)}; a horizon changes the procedure (Wald (3.8)-(3.10), p.127)
thm:p15-se-errors: boundary choice A>=1/alpha, B<=beta guarantees both targets for the actual errors (Wald (3.16)-(3.23), p.129)
thm:p15-se-nominal: nominal boundaries A=(1-beta)/alpha, B=beta/(1-alpha), their exact consequences and a one-step counterexample (Wald (3.24)-(3.30), pp.131-132)

components.gap: Every approximation the handbook itself uses is explained, but the success condition is not plainly met across the selected source extent ('complete original ... stopping/error and sample-size arguments'). Inside ranges the handbook cites, Wald states that for a score law not on a lattice, gamma (p.136, in Section 3.4 between (3.44) and (3.45); Section 3.4 is cited at line 273) and E Z_n, hence E(n) (p.143, between (4.7) and (4.8), within (4.4)-(4.14) cited at line 218), can be approximated arbitrarily finely by replacing z with a discrete lattice law of small span. The handbook gives exact calculation only for lattice laws (lines 276-317) and finite-horizon prefix enumeration only for a finite nonlattice alphabet (lines 314-316). The annex (lines 242-248) rejects an 'unqualified grid approximation' without stating it. For continuous score laws, including the normal case the source works through, the handbook never says what the discretized calculation computes. That calculation concerns a different score law, so a different stopping procedure, and the handbook leaves open whether, or when, its gamma and E(T) apply to the actual procedure. Also left unexplained from the cited ranges: the claim that gamma-bar minus gamma tends to zero as the score mean and variance tend to zero (p.135); the use of (4.51) when B>0 and the upper-exit probability is near one (p.151); and the claim that the nominal boundaries only increase E_i(n), so that Table 1 understates the true saving (pp.133, 146, 148).

evidence.label: thm:p15-se-repeated-fixed: each preselected look has level alpha, the first-rejection rule over M looks has error 1-(1-alpha)^M (.6415 at M=20, one when unbounded), compared with the SPRT with A>=1/alpha whose upper-exit error is at most alpha over the whole horizon
annex:p15.se.repeated-fixed proof
thm:p15-se-errors: the horizon-wide bound used for the valid design
On-route cumulative-look case: exact first-crossing error exceeds alpha from two looks
Calibrated constant threshold c_K with exact level alpha for K looks; none for unbounded looks; the SPRT bound as the horizon-wide alternative

defect_observations.observation: thm:p15-se-dependent cites Wald p.130 but leaves out the source's AR(1) normal instance (lambda_0 != lambda_1, both positive and below 1; x_1 and x_j - lambda_i x_{j-1} independent N(0,1)). For that instance Wald asserts that (3.18)-(3.19) hold for the SPRT. The handbook keeps almost-sure termination as a hypothesis and never verifies it for any dependent process. Not used to fail C03, because the handbook makes no dependent-process claim that it leaves unproved.

def:p15-se-normal-saving says N_fixed is the smallest fixed sample allowing errors no larger than alpha and beta. The annex proof (lines 311-316) shows only that the level-alpha upper test on the sample mean meets beta exactly when sqrt(N)(theta_1-theta_0) >= q_{1-alpha}+q_{1-beta}. It never writes or cross-references the Neyman-Pearson step showing that no other fixed-sample test of smaller size does better, although thm:p15-neyman-pearson is on the route (handbook/parts/p15/hypothesis-tests-and-confidence.tex:95). The source limits n(alpha,beta) to the current most powerful test (p.145).

Mirror-case steps are given by reference instead of written out: 'The upper interval follows similarly' (195-196), 'The below-one value similarly gives' (260-261), 'Applying the same calculation to -X' (292-293), 'in the same calculation' for Re(t)<0 (343-344) and 'by the same argument' for the alternative deadline inequality (418-419). Each is a symmetric restatement whose written argument carries over verbatim, so none is counted here as a missing owed proof. They are recorded for the strict proof standard.

def:p15-se-procedure does not say that R_m^0, R_m^1 and R_m are measurable for a nonrandomized design, yet it asserts {T<=m} in F_m. Measurability is stated only for the randomized extension (line 60).

The quadrilateral step says 'their nonnegative-axis intersections give the other three vertices', but (0,0) is the meeting point of the axes, not an intersection of either bounding line with an axis. The vertex list also presupposes 0<B<1<A, which thm:p15-se-errors gets only from the practical-case convention at lines 91-93.

The source's bounds (3.24)-(3.25) on the exact boundaries A(alpha,beta) and B(alpha,beta) (p.131) are not stated. Neither is its remark that (3.30) becomes strict when a(alpha,beta) > A(alpha,beta) or b(alpha,beta) < B(alpha,beta) (p.133). That at most one target can be exceeded follows from line 162.

Two items from Wald are not given: the derivative system (4.48)-(4.50) for the conditional first moments of n, and the negative-drift, no-upper-boundary variant of (4.51) (c = sigma_z^{-2} Ez log B, p.150). The handbook says only that derivatives at zero give moments (line 417).
